HarborWorks therefore begins graph work by specifying what a vertex, edge, direction, and weight mean.

blocks.text: A dependency network is not necessarily a hierarchy. HarborWorks can have several services depending on one shared resource, two locations connected by multiple links, or a directed relationship that does not imply a return path. A graph represents those possibilities without forcing them into a tree’s single-parent model.

blocks.text: The representation must preserve the distinctions the application cares about. A zero-cost edge is not the same as no edge. Two parallel links are not necessarily one link. An undirected self-loop may be stored once even though a mathematical degree convention counts it twice. Decide these semantics before writing traversal or optimization code; otherwise a later algorithm can be correct for a graph different from the one you intended to model.

topics.title: 13.1.1 Distinguishing Directed and Undirected Graphs
topics.summary: A directed edge from u to v permits movement or dependency in one direction. The reverse edge is a separate fact. An undirected edge represents a symmetric relationship, so an adjacency-list representation usually stores it in both endpoint lists. The example avoids storing the same self-loop twice when both endpoints are identical.

topics.title: 13.1.2 Distinguishing Weighted and Unweighted Graphs
topics.summary: An unweighted graph treats each traversed edge as one step. A weighted graph attaches a value such as distance, cost, delay, or capacity. Those meanings are not interchangeable. A path’s total delay might be a sum; its available bandwidth may depend on the minimum link capacity instead.

blocks.text: The example stores integer weights and permits zero and negative values. That is a representation capability, not permission to use every shortest-path algorithm unchanged. Breadth-first search computes minimum hop counts in an unweighted graph. An algorithm requiring nonnegative weights must validate that stronger precondition at its boundary.

blocks.text: An unweighted graph treats every edge as one step for a hop-count question. A weighted graph attaches a value such as distance, latency, cost, or capacity. The meaning of that number determines which algorithms are valid. A minimum-cost path and a maximum-capacity path are different problems even when both use an integer edge field.

blocks.text: The representation permits zero and negative integer weights. That flexibility does not make every later optimization algorithm applicable. Breadth-first search ignores weights and finds minimum edge count. Dijkstra’s shortest-path method requires nonnegative weights in the routing capstone. A minimum spanning tree can legitimately contain negative-weight edges. Algorithm preconditions belong alongside the algorithm, not hidden inside a generic graph name.

blocks.text: Absence should be represented independently from weight. Using zero to mean “no edge” makes a legitimate zero-weight connection disappear. The matrix view therefore stores optional integers. A present optional containing zero is an edge; an empty optional is no edge. This is the same present-zero distinction already used for map values and optional indices.

blocks.text: Units matter. Adding milliseconds to kilometers yields a number but not a meaningful route cost. A production graph model can use strong domain types or validated metadata to keep units consistent. The teaching example uses plain integers so the representation mechanism remains visible, while the application notes should still state what a weight means.

blocks.text: For path computations, accumulated values need a wider or checked arithmetic domain. Individually valid edge weights can overflow when added along a long path. Bounding vertex count and edge magnitude can justify a safe sum in a selected type; alternatively, perform checked addition. Never infer that a valid int field makes every aggregate int result valid.

blocks.text: The conversion here collapses parallel edges by selecting the smallest weight. That policy is useful for some cost problems but loses multiplicity and all larger parallel weights. It is not a reversible serialization of the adjacency lists. The conversion allocates V² optional cells, initializes them as absent, then examines each stored edge: O(V²+E) time and O(V²) additional space, counting stored adjacency entries.

reading.title: 13.2.1 Building Adjacency Matrices
paragraphs: An adjacency matrix has one cell for each ordered pair of vertices, requiring O(V²) cells even when there are few edges. Endpoint-pair lookup is direct indexing once bounds are checked. Enumerating a vertex’s neighbors scans its row and therefore takes O(V), including absent entries.

An undirected matrix is symmetric when its edge semantics are symmetric. The diagonal can contain self-loops; do not force it to zero or absent without a domain rule. A boolean matrix is enough only when weights and multiplicity are irrelevant.

The conversion here collapses parallel edges by selecting the smallest weight. That policy is useful for some cost problems but loses multiplicity and all larger parallel weights. It is not a reversible serialization of the adjacency lists. The conversion allocates V² optional cells, initializes them as absent, then examines each stored edge: O(V²+E) time and O(V²) additional space, counting stored adjacency entries.

An adjacency matrix assigns a cell to every ordered pair of vertices. For V vertices, it contains V*V cells. A direct edge query can index one cell, but storage grows quadratically even when only a few edges exist. This is why representation choice must consider both query shape and graph density.

The worked conversion creates a matrix of optional weights. It then visits every stored adjacency entry and updates the corresponding cell. Parallel edges are collapsed by retaining the minimum weight. That rule makes sense for some minimum-cost edge queries, but it loses multiplicity and information about more expensive parallel links. It is not a lossless serialization of the adjacency list.

A matrix diagonal is not automatically a zero-length path. The conversion records explicit self-loop edges only. Shortest-path algorithms sometimes initialize a distance matrix diagonal to zero because a vertex can reach itself without traversing an edge. That is an algorithmic distance convention, different from an adjacency representation of actual edges. Keep the two matrices conceptually separate.

Validate scale before conversion in a real application. A sparse graph with one hundred thousand vertices might have a manageable adjacency list and an infeasible dense matrix. Checking only that the original graph fits in memory says nothing about the derived V*V representation. The complete capstone avoids a dense production-sized conversion and uses only tiny dense reference graphs in tests.

Nested vectors add another layout consideration. A vector of row vectors gives each row its own allocation; it is not necessarily one contiguous V*V block. A flattened vector can improve layout predictability but requires checked product and offset arithmetic. Either representation must preserve optional absence and the chosen parallel-edge policy.

When testing conversion, include a zero-weight edge, an absent edge, parallel edges with different weights, and directionality. A matrix containing only positive distinct weights can conceal several of the semantic losses this design is meant to prevent.

blocks.text: Review reasoning. Why can a graph be sparse yet have an enormous matrix? The matrix reserves a cell for every possible pair. Why does a zero diagonal have different meanings in adjacency and distance matrices? One records actual edges; the other may include empty paths. Why are nonnegative weights a separate algorithm precondition? Different algorithms interpret weights differently. Why does two-sided capacity preparation not preserve all borrows? Reallocation can occur before logical publication. Why is exact per-edge reserve undesirable? It can replace geometric growth with repeated linear relocation.
